questions.prompt: What do generics allow you to write in Swift?

options.text: Flexible and reusable functions and types that work with any type.
options.explanation: Right. Generics enable reusable code that works with any type while preserving type safety.

options.text: Functions that bypass compile-time type checking entirely.
options.explanation: Generics enforce strict compile-time type checking.

options.text: Dynamic closures that execute only on secondary threads.
options.explanation: Generics are static type abstractions, unrelated to thread scheduling.

options.text: Classes that inherit from multiple superclasses simultaneously.
options.explanation: Swift classes only support single inheritance, regardless of generics.

questions.prompt: How are type parameter placeholders declared on a generic function?

options.text: Inside parentheses after the parameter names.
options.explanation: Parentheses enclose function arguments, not type parameters.

options.text: Inside angle brackets immediately after the function name.
options.explanation: Right. Type parameters are written in angle brackets, like func swapTwo<T>(...).

options.text: Inside square brackets before the return arrow.
options.explanation: Square brackets define array types and collection subscripts.

options.text: Inside curly braces preceding the function body.
options.explanation: Curly braces enclose the executable body statements.

options.text: Array only.
options.explanation: Dictionary and Set are also generic collection types.

options.text: Dictionary only.
options.explanation: Array and Set are also built as generic collections.

options.text: Array, Set, and Dictionary.

options.text: None of the standard collections use generics.
options.explanation: Swift standard collections are foundational examples of generic types.

questions.prompt: What is a type constraint in Swift generics?

options.text: A rule restricting functions to accept only integer types.
options.explanation: Type constraints apply to arbitrary protocols or class hierarchies.

options.text: A compiler limit capping generic parameters at four.
options.explanation: Swift enforces no arbitrary limit on generic parameter count.

options.text: A check that converts value types to heap references.
options.explanation: Constraints define interface requirements, not memory allocation.

options.text: A requirement that a type parameter conform to a protocol or class.
options.explanation: Right. Syntax like <T: Equatable> enforces protocol or superclass conformance.

questions.prompt: Why does a generic function comparing elements with == require <T: Equatable>?

options.text: Because not all Swift types support the == operator by default.
options.explanation: Right. The compiler requires the Equatable constraint to verify that == is valid.

options.text: Because Equatable converts objects to numeric hashes.
options.explanation: Hashable generates integer hashes, while Equatable provides equality.

options.text: Because unconstrained generics cannot be compiled into machine code.
options.explanation: Unconstrained generics compile cleanly, but cannot use ==.

options.text: Because Equatable is required for all function arguments.
options.explanation: Functions only require Equatable when equality comparisons occur.

questions.prompt: How do you extend a generic type named Stack<Element> in Swift?

options.text: extension Stack<Element> { ... }
options.explanation: Swift forbids repeating type parameter angle brackets on extensions.

options.text: extension Stack { ... }
options.explanation: Right. You write extension Stack and use Element directly in the body.

options.text: extension Stack where Element: Any { ... }
options.explanation: Unconstrained extensions do not require redundant where clauses.

options.text: extension <Element> Stack { ... }
options.explanation: This syntax is invalid in the Swift programming language.

questions.prompt: Why are Swift generics superior to using Any for general collections?

options.text: Any collections execute on background threads only.
options.explanation: Any has no effect on thread scheduling.

options.text: Any collections cannot be mutated after creation.
options.explanation: Variables of type [Any] can be mutated freely.

options.text: Generics guarantee static type safety without runtime casting.
options.explanation: Right. Generics catch type mismatches at compile time, eliminating runtime casts.

options.text: Generics eliminate the need for memory management.
options.explanation: ARC manages memory for generic types just like concrete types.

questions.prompt: How does the Swift compiler optimize generic functions during compilation?

options.text: By converting all generic parameters to Objective-C id pointers.
options.explanation: Pure Swift generics do not box types into Objective-C pointers.

options.text: By interpreting generic method calls through a bytecode virtual machine.
options.explanation: Swift compiles to native machine code, not interpreted bytecode.

options.text: By erasing all generic types to raw untyped heap blocks.
options.explanation: Java uses type erasure; Swift preserves full type metadata.

options.text: By specializing functions for concrete types (monomorphization).
options.explanation: Right. Compiler specialization produces direct machine code for concrete types.

questions.prompt: What is a trade-off of aggressive compiler generic specialization (monomorphization)?

options.text: It causes memory retain cycles between value types.
options.explanation: Specialization does not introduce ARC retain cycles.

options.text: It forces code to run on a single background queue.
options.explanation: Generics have no correlation with Grand Central Dispatch queues.

options.text: It can increase the final binary code size.
options.explanation: Right. Generating specialized machine code for many types increases binary size.

options.text: It disables compile-time type checking.
options.explanation: Monomorphization relies on strict compile-time type verification.

questions.prompt: Explain what generics are in Swift, how type parameters work, and why generics are preferred over Any.

rubric.criterion: Explains that generics allow writing flexible, reusable code with placeholder type parameters (like <T>)
Contrasts with Any, noting generics maintain compile-time type safety without runtime casting
Mentions that standard Swift collections like Array and Dictionary are generic types

questions.modelAnswer: Generics enable you to write flexible, reusable functions and types that work with any type using placeholder names in angle brackets like <T>. Unlike Any, generics enforce strict compile-time static type safety without requiring runtime downcasts. Standard collections like Array and Dictionary are built using generics.

questions.prompt: What are type constraints in Swift generics, and why are they necessary when using operators like == or < inside generic functions?

rubric.criterion: Explains that type constraints specify that a type parameter must inherit from a class or conform to a protocol
Explains that operators like == or < require protocol conformance (such as Equatable or Comparable) to be permitted by the compiler

questions.modelAnswer: Type constraints specify that a generic type parameter must inherit from a specific class or conform to a protocol, such as <T: Equatable>. Because arbitrary Swift types do not automatically support comparison operators, type constraints are necessary to prove to the compiler that operators like == or < are supported.

questions.prompt: How do you extend a generic type, and what syntax rule applies to the type parameter list?

rubric.criterion: Explains that extensions use the type name without angle brackets (for example, extension Stack)
Explains that the existing type parameter placeholders (like Element) are available inside the extension body automatically

questions.modelAnswer: When extending a generic type, you do not restate the type parameter list in angle brackets; you simply write extension TypeName. The original type parameter placeholders (such as Element) are automatically available inside the extension body for properties and methods.

questions.prompt: Explain compiler specialization (monomorphization) in Swift generics and its performance benefits.

rubric.criterion: Explains that the compiler generates specialized machine code for concrete types used at call sites
Explains that specialization eliminates runtime boxing and indirection, matching the performance of hand-written concrete code

questions.modelAnswer: Compiler specialization (monomorphization) generates concrete, non-generic machine code for each specific type used at call sites. This optimization eliminates runtime boxing and indirect table dispatch, allowing the generic function to execute at the speed of hand-written concrete functions.

questions.prompt: How do generic where clauses work, and when should you use them instead of simple protocol constraints?

rubric.criterion: Explains that where clauses define complex requirements across multiple parameters or associated types
Gives an example such as equating associated types or adding conditional protocol conformances

questions.modelAnswer: A generic where clause defines requirements for type parameters and associated types. Simple constraints like <T: Equatable> work for single types. Where clauses handle multi-type relationships, like matching elements between two collections.

questions.prompt: Write a generic function swapValues<T> that swaps the values of two inout parameters of type T.
questions.modelAnswer:
func swapValues<T>(_ a: inout T, _ b: inout T) {
    let temp = a
    a = b
    b = temp
}
var x = 10
var y = 20
swapValues(&x, &y)
print("\(x) and \(y)")

rubric.criterion: Declares generic function signature with type parameter <T> and inout parameters
Correctly swaps both inout values using a temporary constant
